# DEFLATION-BASED SPECTRAL PRECONDITIONING FOR THE CONJUGATE GRADIENT METHOD ON PERTURBED SYSTEMS <sup>∗</sup>

Y. DIOUANE<sup>†</sup>, S. GÜROL<sup>‡</sup>, O. MOUHTAL<sup>‡†</sup>, AND D. ORBAN<sup>†</sup>

**Abstract.** We consider sequences of large symmetric positive-definite linear systems in which spectral information from a reference matrix _A_ is reused to accelerate the solution of a nearby system with perturbed matrix _A(t_)=_A+tE_, where _E_ is symmetric, \(\|E\|_F=1\), and \(t\ge 0\) is the perturbation size. We compare deflated conjugate gradient (deflated CG) with preconditioned CG (PCG) equipped with a scaled spectral preconditioner constructed from the same spectral information of _A_. First, we derive an energy-norm error characterization of deflated CG. We then use perturbation analysis to show that, after one additional PCG iteration, the squared PCG error is bounded, up to terms of order _t_<sup>2</sup>, by an explicit multiple of the squared deflated CG error. This result clarifies the role of the scaling parameter in the preconditioner. Experiments show that the scaled spectral preconditioner recovers much of the convergence improvement provided by deflation while requiring fewer products with _A(t_).

**Key words.** Krylov methods, conjugate gradient, PCG, deflated CG, spectral preconditioner.

**MSC codes.** 65F08, 65F22, 65F15

**1. Introduction.** We consider sequences of large symmetric positive-definite (SPD) linear systems solved by the conjugate gradient (CG) method [15]. Such sequences arise in many applications, such as variational data assimilation [8], where consecutive systems are often closely related. Information generated while solving one system can then be recycled to accelerate subsequent solves; see, for example, [12, 22, 25, 28].

We consider a reference matrix _A_ together with a nearby matrix _A(t_)=_A+tE_, where _E_ is symmetric, \(\|E\|_F=1\), and _t_ is sufficiently small for _A(t_) to remain positive definite. Our goal is to reuse spectral information from _A_ to accelerate CG applied to the perturbed system _A(t)x=b_. This is particularly attractive in large-scale matrix- free settings, where constructing a preconditioner may be prohibitively expensive and only a limited number of matrix-vector products can be afforded.

One important approach for exploiting recycled information is deflated CG. Given a deflation subspace W=Range(_W_), deflated CG splits the solution into a component in W and a complementary component computed by CG on a projected system [9, 21, 24]. Tang et al. [27] mention that, for any deflation subspace, the effective condition number of the deflated system does not exceed that of the original system. A widely used choice for the deflation subspace is a set of approximate eigenvectors obtained from previous Krylov iterations through Ritz or harmonic Ritz projections [22, 24, 25, 29]. In the nonsymmetric setting, SVD-based strategies have also been proposed for recycling Krylov subspaces, in particular for GMRES [1]. Problem-dependent alternatives include coarse spaces arising from domain decomposition and multilevel methods [27]. These approaches seek to construct a low-dimensional subspace that captures the components responsible for slow convergence at moderate additional cost.

<tbc>Approaches related to deflation are limited-memory preconditioners (LMPs) [13], augmentation methods [10], balancing strategies [20], and low-rank updates [3]. When spectral information is used in the preconditioner, we refer to such methods as spectral preconditioners [5, 11, 13]. For broader overviews of preconditioning, see [2, 23, 30].

The effect of using approximate spectral information has therefore received considerable attention. The sensitivity of deflated CG to perturbations of the deflation subspace is studied in [17], while Giraud and Gratton [11] analyze how errors in approximate eigenpairs affect the spectrum of the preconditioned matrix. These results characterize the influence of inexact spectral information on the projected or preconditioned spectrum. Although deflation can significantly improve CG convergence, its construction may become costly when the coefficient matrix changes. For a deflation basis \(W\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times k}\), one must form and solve a system with the matrix \(W^\top A(t)W\), which requires additional products with _A(t_). This problem generally needs to be solved accurately, since the convergence of deflated CG can be sensitive to errors in its solution [20]. To mitigate this sensitivity, related approaches avoid mapping the selected eigenvalues to zero, e.g., Erlangga and Nabben [7] shift selected eigenvalues to a nonzero part of the spectrum and use the resulting preconditioner within GMRES.

In [6], the authors introduced a scaled spectral preconditioner designed to reduce the energy-norm error after a prescribed number of preconditioned CG (PCG) iterations. The preconditioner is constructed from the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of _A_ and maps the selected eigenvalues to a common value \(\theta\). Experiments showed that an appropriate choice of the scaling parameter can reproduce much of the convergence acceleration obtained with deflation while requiring a lower initialization cost. In particular, this behavior was observed in a data assimilation problem when approximate eigenpairs were recycled. However, the theoretical analysis in [6] assumes that the spectral information used to construct the preconditioner is exact and is associated with the matrix of the system being solved. It therefore does not explain why similar behavior persists when spectral information from a nearby matrix is reused.

Our main objective in this work is to establish this connection theoretically when spectral information obtained from _A_ is reused for the perturbed system _A(t)x=b_. We focus on eigenpairs associated with the largest eigenvalues of _A_, although the analysis extends to any selected subset of eigenpairs. We compare the energy-norm errors generated by deflated CG and by PCG equipped with the scaled spectral preconditioner. Using first-order perturbation analysis, we show that, after one additional PCG iteration, the squared energy-norm error of PCG is bounded by the squared energy-norm error of deflated CG multiplied by an explicit factor, plus higher- order terms in _t_. The resulting bound clarifies how the scaling parameter \(\theta\) should be chosen relative to the nondeflated spectrum and provides a theoretical explanation for the similar convergence behavior observed numerically. We complement the theoretical analysis with numerical experiments on synthetic linear systems.

The paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we review deflated CG and derive a characterization of its energy-norm error. We formulate the perturbed problem, develop the first-order analysis, establish the comparison between PCG and deflated CG, and discuss practical choices of the scaling parameter in Section 3. We report the numerical experiments in Section 4 and present our conclusions in Section 5.

**Notation:** The spectral norm of a matrix _X_ is denoted \(\|\|_2\), its spectral radius \(\rho(X)\), and its range R(_X_). For a symmetric matrix \(X\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\), we denote its eigenvalues \(\lambda_1(X),\dots,\lambda_n(X)\) and the corresponding eigenvectors _s_<sub>1</sub>(_X),...,s<sub>n</sub>(X_). Throughout the paper, \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) is SPD. When there is no ambiguity, its _i_th eigenvalue and corresponding eigenvector are denoted \(\lambda_i\) and _s<sub>i</sub>_, respectively. For \(k\in\{1,\dots,n-1\}\),

<tbc>we define \(S_k=[s_1,\dots,s_k]\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times k}\) and \(\overline{S_k}=[s_{k+1},\dots,s_n]\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times(n-k)}\). Thus, _S<sub>k</sub>_ contains the eigenvectors associated with the _k_ largest eigenvalues of _A_, while the columns of <o>_S_</o><sub>k</sub> span the orthogonal complement of R(_S<sub>k</sub>_). For \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\), the _A_-norm, also called the _energy norm_, is defined by \(\|x\|_A=\sqrt{x^\top Ax}\). We denote \(\mathbb{P}_\ell(0)\) the set of polynomials of degree at most \(\ell\) with value 1 at zero.

In what follows, all results are derived under the assumption of exact arithmetic.

**2. Deflated conjugate gradient.** Let \(W\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times k}\) have full column rank. Deflated CG \[9, 24\] decomposes the solution of _Ax=b_ into a component in the deflation subspace R(_W_) and a complementary component computed by CG on a projected system. Let _V=AW_ and define the projection \(P=I_n-V\big(W^\top V\big)^{-1}W^\top\). Deflated CG then generates iterates of the form \[24\]<tbc>

(2.1) \(x_\ell^\mathrm{D}=W\big(W^\top V\big)^{-1}W^\top b+P^\top z_\ell,\)

<tbc>where \(z_\ell\) are the iterates of CG applied to the projected system<tbc>

(2.2) \(\widehat{A}z=\widehat{b},\)

<tbc>with \(\widehat{A}=PA\), \(\widehat{b}=Pb\), and arbitrary starting vector _z_<sub>0</sub>. The projected system (2.2) can be solved by CG \[18\], since \(\widehat{A}\) is symmetric positive semidefinite, satisfies \(\mathrm{dim}(\mathcal{R}(\widehat{A}))=n-k\) \[24\], and \(\widehat{b}\in\mathcal{R}(\widehat{A})\). Consider the eigen-decomposition<tbc>

\(\widehat{A}=[Q_k\overline{Q_k}]\left[\begin{array}{ c c }
0 & 0 \\
0 & \overline{\Delta_k}
\end{array}\right][Q_k\overline{Q_k}]^\top,\)

<tbc>where \(Q_k\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times k}\) spans the nullspace of \(\widehat{A}\), \(\overline{\Delta_k}\in\mathbb{R}^{(n-k)\times(n-k)}\) is diagonal of nonzero eigenvalues of \(\widehat{A}\), and \(\overline{Q_k}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times(n-k)}\) the corresponding eigenvectors. In the next lemma, we show that solving (2.2) is equivalent to solving the reduced system

(2.3) \(\overline{\Delta_k}\widetilde{y}=\widetilde{b},\text{where}\widetilde{b}=\overline{Q_k^\top\widehat{b}}.\)

Lemma 2.1. _Let_ \(\{z_\ell\}\) _be the iterates generated by CG applied to_ (2.2) _with an initial vector z_<sub>0</sub>_, and let_ \(\{\widetilde{y}_\ell\}\) _be the iterates generated by CG applied to_ (2.3) _with initial vector_ \(\widetilde{y}_0=\overline{Q_k^\top z_0}\)_. Let_ \(\widetilde{r}_\ell\) _and_ \(\widetilde{p}_\ell\) _be the residuals and search directions when solving_ (2.3) _with CG, and_ \(\widehat{r}_\ell\) _and_ \(\widehat{p}_\ell\) _be the residuals and search directions when solving_ (2.2) _with CG. Then, for every_ \(\ell\in\{0,\dots,n-k\}\) _such that_ \(\widetilde{y}_\ell\) _exists,_

(2.4) \(\widetilde{r}_\ell=\overline{Q_k^\top\widehat{r}_\ell}\text{\textit{and}}\widehat{r}_\ell\in\mathcal{R}(\widehat{A})=\mathcal{R}(\overline{Q_k}),\)

(2.5) \(\widetilde{p}_\ell=\overline{Q_k^\top\widehat{p}_\ell}\text{\textit{and}}\widehat{p}_\ell\in\mathcal{R}(\widehat{A}),\)

(2.6) \(\widetilde{y}_\ell=\overline{Q_k^\top z_\ell},\)

(2.7) \(Q_kQ_k^\top z_\ell=Q_kQ_k^\top z_0.\)

_Proof._ We proceed by induction. For \(\ell=0\),

\(\widetilde{r}_0=\overline{Q_k^\top\widehat{b}}-\overline{\Delta_k}\widetilde{y}_0=\overline{Q_k^\top}(\widehat{b}-\overline{Q_k}\overline{\Delta_k}\overline{Q_k^\top z_0})=\overline{Q_k^\top}(\widehat{b}-\widehat{A}z_0)=\overline{Q_k^\top\widehat{r}_0}.\)

Because the projected system is consistent, \(\widehat{b}\in\mathcal{R}(\widehat{A})\); hence \(\widehat{r}_0\in\mathcal{R}(\widehat{A})\). Furthermore, \(\widetilde{p}_0=\widetilde{r}_0\) and \(\widehat{p}_0=\widehat{r}_0\), so \(\widetilde{p}_0=\overline{Q_k^\top\widehat{p}_0}\). The identities (2.6) and (2.7) hold at \(\ell=0\) by

definition. Assume now that (2.4)-(2.7) hold at iteration \(\ell \(=\overline{Q_k^\top}\left(\widehat{r}_{\ell+1}+\frac{\widehat{r}_{\ell+1}^\top\widehat{r}_{\ell+1}}{\widehat{r}_\ell^\top\widehat{r}_\ell}\widehat{p}_\ell\right)=\overline{Q_k^\top}\widehat{p}_{\ell+1}.\) Since \(\widehat{p}_{\ell+1}\) is a linear combination of \(\widehat{p}_\ell\) and \(\widehat{r}_{\ell+1}\), it also belongs to \(\mathcal{R}(\widehat{A})\). Finally, \(Q_kQ_k^\top\widehat{p}_\ell=0\), so the null-space component of \(z_{\ell+1}\) remains equal to that of _z_0. This proves (2.7) and completes the induction. □ In exact arithmetic, CG finds the exact solution \(\widehat{y}^*\) of (2.3) in at most _n-k_ iterations. From (2.6) and (2.7), the corresponding final iterate for (2.2) is (2.8) \(z^*=Q_kQ_k^\top z_0+\overline{Q_k}\overline{\Delta_k^{-1}}\overline{Q_k^\top\widehat{b}}.\) The first term in (2.8) is the component of the initial vector _z_0 in the null space of \(\widehat{A}\). By (2.7), in exact arithmetic, CG leaves it unchanged. The second term is the uniquely determined component in \(\mathcal{R}(\widehat{A})\) that solves the projected system (2.2). Assuming that the_ \(\ell\)_-th deflated CG iterate_ \(x_\ell^D\) _exists, the corresponding error satisfies_ \(\left\|x^*-x_\ell^D\right\|_A^2=min_{p\in\mathbb{P}_\ell(0)}\|p(\overline{\Delta_k})\left(\widetilde{y}^*-\widetilde{y}_0\right)\|_{\overline{\Delta_k}}^2=min_{p\in\mathbb{P}_\ell(0)}\|p(\overline{\Delta_k})\overline{Q_k^\top}\left(z^*-z_0\right)\|_{\overline{\Delta_k}}^2,\) _where x_∗ _represents the exact solution of Ax=b and_ \(\widetilde{y}_0=\overline{Q_k^\top} z_0\). _Proof._ Applying (2.1) to both \(x_\ell^\mathrm{D}\) and the exact solution _x_∗ (with \(z_\ell\) replaced by _z_∗), and using \(PAP^\top=PA=\overline{Q_k}\overline{\Delta_k}\overline{Q_k^\top}\) (see \[9\]) gives \(\left\|x^*-x_\ell^\mathrm{D}\right\|_A^2=\left\|P^\top\left(z^*-z_\ell\right)\right\|_A^2=\left(z^*-z_\ell\right)^\top PAP^\top\left(z^*-z_\ell\right)\)
\(=\left(z^*-z_\ell\right)^\top PA\left(z^*-z_\ell\right)\)
\(=\left(z^*-z_\ell\right)^\top\overline{Q_k}\overline{\Delta_k}\overline{Q_k^\top}\left(z^*-z_\ell\right)\)
\(=\left\|\overline{Q_k^\top}(z^*-z_\ell)\right\|_{\overline{\Delta_k}}^2=\left\|\widetilde{y}^*-\widetilde{y}_\ell\right\|_{\overline{\Delta_k}}^2.\)

**3. Deflated CG and PCG for a perturbed system.** Let _A(t_)=_A+tE_, where \(t\ge 0\) and _E_ is symmetric with \(\|E\|_F=1\). Since _A_ is SPD, _A(t_) is SPD for sufficiently small values of _t_. In this section, we compare the scaled spectral preconditioner in \[6\] with deflated CG when solving the perturbed linear system<tbc>

(3.1) \(A(t)x=b.\)

<tbc>Let \(1\le k\le n-1\). For deflated CG, we use the subspace _W=S<sub>k</sub>_=\[_s_<sub>1</sub>_,...,s<sub>k</sub>_\], formed by the eigenvectors associated with the _k_ largest eigenvalues \(\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\dots,\lambda_k\) of _A_. Set _V(t_)=_A(t)S<sub>k</sub>_ and \(P(t)=I_n-V(t)\left(S_k^\top V(t)\right)^{-1}S_k^\top\). The projected system is<tbc>

(3.2) \(\widehat{A}(t)z=\widehat{b}(t),\)

<tbc>where \(\widehat{A}(t):=P(t)A(t)\) and \(\widehat{b}(t):=P(t)b\). The \(\ell\)-th iterate of deflated CG is given by

(3.3) \(x_\ell^{[\mathrm{D}]}(t)=S_k\left(S_k^\top V(t)\right)^{-1}S_k^\top b+P(t)^\top z_\ell(t),\)

where \(z_\ell(t)\) is the iterate of CG when solving (3.2).

Let \(\theta>0\) and \(\Lambda_k:=\mathrm{diag}(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_k)\), the scaled spectral preconditioner is defined by \(U^\theta=I_n+S_k\left(\sqrt{\theta}\Lambda_k^{-1/2}-I_k\right)S_k^\top\). The associated preconditioned system is

(3.4) \(U^\theta A(t)U^\theta y=U^\theta b,x=U^\theta y.\)

Similarly, the \(\ell\)th iterate of PCG is \(x_\ell^{[\mathrm{P}]}(t)=U^\theta y_\ell(t)\), where \(y_\ell(t)\) is the iterate of CG when solving (3.4) starting from _y_<sub>0</sub>.

**3.1. Perturbation analysis.** In this section, we introduce the perturbation results to quantify how eigenvalues and eigenvectors change with _t_ and to control the gap terms in our subsequent comparison of the energy-norm errors of PCG and deflated CG. We first recall the first-order perturbation theory for simple eigenvalues and eigenvectors of symmetric matrices. These classical results (see, e.g., \[26\]) describe how the eigenpairs \(\{\lambda_i(t),s_i(t)\}\) of _A(t_) evolve with small _t_. For _i_=1_,...,n_ and if \(\lambda_i\) is simple, then

(3.5) \(\lambda_i(t)=\lambda_i+ts_i^\top Es_i+O(t^2),s_i(t)=s_i+t\underline{S_i}(\lambda_iI_{n-1}-\underline{\underline{\Lambda_i}})^{-1}\underline{S_i^\top} Es_i+O(t^2),\)

where \(\underline{\underline{\Lambda_i}}=\mathrm{diag}(\lambda_j)_{j\neq i}\), and \(\underline{S_i}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times(n-1)}\) is obtained by removing the _i_th column from the eigenvector matrix of _A_. Second-order remainder estimates for eigenpairs are known; see, e.g., \[19, Ch. II\]. For our analysis, we provide a short self-contained proof for symmetric matrices. The resulting bound involves only concrete constants and an explicit range of validity for _t_, both expressed in terms of the spectral gap, without relying on contour integration.

Proposition 3.1. _Let_ \(i\in\{1,\dots,n\}\)_, and assume that_ \(\lambda_i\) _is simple. Let_ \(g_i:=\mathrm{min}_{j\neq i}|\lambda_i-\lambda_j|>0\) _be the spectral gap around_ \(\lambda_i\)_. Then, for every_ \(t\in[0,g_i/(4\|E\|_2)]\)_, A(t_) _admits a simple eigenpair_ \(\{\lambda_i(t),s_i(t)\}\) _such that_<tbc>

\(\left|\lambda_i(t)-\lambda_i-ts_i^\top Es_i\right|\le\frac{4\|E\|_2^2}{g_i}t^2,\left\|s_i(t)-s_i-t\underline{S_i}(\lambda_iI_{n-1}-\underline{\underline{\Lambda_i}})^{-1}\underline{S_i^\top} Es_i\right\|_2\le\frac{12\|E\|_2^2}{g_i^2}t^2.\)

Hence, for \(0\le t\le g_i/(2\left\|E\right\|_2)\), \(|\lambda_i(t)-\lambda_i|\le g_i/2\). Since, for every \(j\neq i\), \(|\lambda_i-\lambda_j|\ge g_i\), this gives

(3.14) \(0\le 1-a(t)=\frac{\left\|d(t)\right\|_2^2}{1+a(t)}\le\left\|d(t)\right\|_2^2\le\frac{4t^2\left\|E\right\|_2^2}{g_i^2}.\)

Theorem 3.8 provides an explicit second-order comparison between PCG with \(U^\theta\) and deflated CG. After one additional PCG iteration, the squared energy-norm error is bounded by the squared deflated CG error multiplied by \((\alpha(t,\theta)/\theta)^2\), plus a remainder of order _t_<sup>2</sup>. The quantity \(\alpha(t,\theta)\) is the largest distance from \(\theta\) to the nonzero eigenvalues of \(\widehat{A}(t)\); by Lemma 3.3, these eigenvalues agree with the corresponding eigenvalues of _A(t_) up to _O(t_<sup>2</sup>). Thus, if \(\alpha(t,\theta)/\theta<1\), the leading term is contractive.

The explicit factor \(\gamma_1q_k^{2\ell}+\gamma_2\ell q_k^{2\ell-1}\) describes how the perturbation remainder depends on the iteration index. When _q<sub>k</sub>\>_1, this upper bound can grow rapidly with \(\ell\) and can be pessimistic; when 0_\<q<sub>k</sub>\<_1, its behavior is different and it may decrease as \(\ell\) grows. This concerns only the quality of the perturbation estimate and does not imply that either iterative method has increasing error. Increasing _k_ removes more eigenvalues from the nondeflated spectrum and may reduce _q<sub>k</sub>_.

**4. Numerical experiments.**

## 4.1. Computational complexity: PCG versus deflated CG.

Assume that _S<sub>k</sub>_=\[_s_<sub>1</sub>_,...,s<sub>k</sub>_\] and \(\Lambda_k=\mathrm{diag}(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_k)\) are available. Both deflated CG and PCG with \(U^\theta\) use CG as an iterative solver; the main computational difference lies in the cost of applying the deflation projector versus applying the scaled spectral preconditioner.

Deflated CG requires the projector \(P(t)=I_n-V_k(t)\left(S_k^\top V_k(t)\right)^{-1}S_k^\top\), where _V<sub>k</sub>(t_)=_A(t)S<sub>k</sub>_. Constructing this projector requires _k_ products with _A(t_) to form _V<sub>k</sub>(t_), O(_nk_<sup>2</sup>) operations to assemble \(S_k^\top V_k(t)\), and O(_k_<sup>3</sup>) operations to factorize it. Once these quantities are available, applying _P(t_) requires products with \(S_k^\top\) and _V<sub>k</sub>(t_) and the solution of a \(k\times k\) linear system. Deflated CG stores _S<sub>k</sub>_, _V<sub>k</sub>(t_), and the dense matrix \(S_k^\top V_k(t)\). In contrast, PCG with the scaled spectral preconditioner \(U^\theta\) stores only _S<sub>k</sub>_, the associated eigenvalues, and the scalar parameter \(\theta\). Applying \(U^\theta\) requires one multiplication by each of \(S_k^\top\) and _S<sub>k</sub>_, together with a diagonal scaling.

**5. Conclusion.** We analyzed sequences of SPD linear systems in which spectral information from a reference matrix _A_ with simple eigenvalues is reused for a perturbed matrix _A(t_)=_A+tE_. Our comparison considered deflated CG and PCG equipped with a scaled spectral preconditioner constructed from the same selected eigenvectors of _A_.

An energy-norm characterization of deflated CG, combined with first-order perturbation analysis, yields an asymptotic comparison of the two methods. After one additional PCG iteration, the squared PCG error is bounded, up to higher-order perturbation terms, by an explicit multiple of the squared deflated CG error. The analysis also motivates the scaling parameter \(\theta_m\). Numerical experiments show that the scaled spectral preconditioner closely reproduces the convergence of deflated CG while avoiding the construction of the deflation projector and its associated products with the perturbed matrix. PCG with this preconditioner is therefore a promising alternative to deflation for sequences of closely related large-scale systems.

An important direction for future work is to extend the perturbation analysis to SPD matrices with multiple eigenvalues. We also fix the perturbation direction _E_ and vary only its magnitude _t_; allowing _E_ to vary and deriving bounds over a class of symmetric perturbations would yield a more general analysis.
